title: Setup words
teaches: The names on our setup list and what each one means: the Kicker, Oops Reversal, Slingshot, Launchpad, High Volume Edge (HVC), Gap Support and the Go Signal, the catalog family each sits in, the Bear gap lesson, and the plan words every setup carries: trigger, stop, R, a third off at 3R and at 5R, the stop to breakeven, partials, trail.

facts.quote: Bullish kickers start with a bearish candle and then show a bullish gap up. Bearish kickers start with a bullish candle and then show a bearish gap down.
facts.claim: A bullish kicker is a down candle followed by a gap up; the bearish kicker is the mirror image.

facts.quote: A kicker pattern is a two-bar candlestick pattern indicating a reversal in an asset's price trend.
facts.claim: Textbooks treat the kicker as a two-candle reversal pattern.

facts.quote: Kicker patterns are rare but highly reliable indicators of market sentiment shifts.
facts.claim: Investopedia calls kickers rare but highly reliable.

facts.quote: Look for a tall black marubozu candle followed by an upward gap then a tall white marubozu candle.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's bullish kicking: a tall black candle, an upward gap, then a tall white candle, both marubozu.

facts.quote: The bullish kicking candle acts as a bullish reversal of the existing price trend 53% of the time. That is almost random, so do not try to guess the breakout direction from this candle pattern.
facts.claim: In Bulkowski's tests the bullish kicking candle reversed the trend 53% of the time, which he calls almost random.

facts.quote: two marubozu's with a gap between is a rare combination, ranking 100th out of 103 candle types
facts.claim: The bullish kicking candle is rare: 100th of 103 candle types by frequency.

facts.quote: The opening range refers to a security's high and low prices during the first 15 minutes of trading.
facts.claim: Investopedia defines the opening range as the high and low of the first 15 minutes.

facts.quote: Day traders frequently use the trading range of the first half hour of the trading session as a reference point for their intraday strategies. For example, a trader might buy a stock if it breaks above its opening trading range.
facts.claim: Day traders often use the first half hour's range and buy a break above it.

facts.quote: Traders may decide to take profits using a multiple of risk. For example, if using a 30-cent stop, traders might set a 60-cent profit target.
facts.claim: Investopedia: traders may take profits at a multiple of risk, such as a 60-cent target on a 30-cent stop.

facts.quote: large increases in trading volume are usually the work of institutional investors, buying or selling
facts.claim: Big jumps in volume are usually institutions buying or selling.

facts.quote: Lack of volume shows the level is not important or that the big traders (who create big volume) aren't ready to participate yet.
facts.claim: Investopedia: big traders create big volume, and a lack of volume can mean they aren't ready to take part yet.

facts.quote: Gaps are places of weak support or resistance, but you can use them for a stop location. Place a stop a few cents below the gap (upward breakouts) or above the gap (downward breakouts).
facts.claim: A gap is weak support, but it works as a stop location: a few cents below an up gap.

facts.quote: As the price of the security moves in a favorable direction the trailing stop price adjusts or “trails” the market price of the security by the specified amount.
facts.claim: A trailing stop moves up behind the price as the trade works.

facts.quote: However, if the security’s price moves in an unfavorable direction the trailing stop price remains fixed
facts.claim: When price moves against you, a trailing stop stays where it is.

facts.quote: A trailing stop is simply a stop order that automatically follows—or trails—the market once the price of a security has initially begun moving in a favorable direction.
facts.claim: A trailing stop follows the price once the trade starts working.

facts.quote: A close above or below a specific moving average, such as the eight-, 20-, or 50-day trailing stops.
facts.claim: A close through a set moving average is one common way to trail a stop.

facts.quote: if the market recently found support or resistance during a healthy pullback to a certain price level, a break below or above that level would be a strong exit signal
facts.claim: A break of the low a healthy pullback just made is a strong exit signal, so a stop can go there.

facts.quote: The uptrend is therefore composed of higher swing lows and higher swing highs. As long as the price is making these higher swing lows and higher swing highs, the uptrend is considered intact.
facts.claim: An uptrend is a run of higher swing lows and higher swing highs; it is intact while they keep coming.

facts.quote: The ATR shows investors the average range of prices for an investment over a specified period.
facts.claim: ATR is the average size of a stock's price range over a set period.

facts.quote: Breakouts with relatively high volume show conviction and interest, and therefore the price is more likely to continue moving in the breakout direction.
facts.claim: Investopedia: breakouts on relatively high volume show conviction and are more likely to keep going.

facts.quote: A buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price.
facts.claim: A buy stop sits above the current price.

facts.quote: Investors generally use a buy stop order in an attempt to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short.
facts.claim: A buy stop is what guards a short position.

facts.quote: R represents your initial risk per unit. It is simply the initial risk per share of stock, or futures contract, or minimum investment unit.
facts.claim: R is your initial risk per share.

facts.quote: You buy a stock at $50 and decide to sell it if it drops to $40. What’s your initial risk? Your initial risk is $10 per share, so in this case, 1R is equal to $10.
facts.claim: Tharp's example: buy at $50 with the exit at $40, and 1R is $10 a share, entry to stop.

facts.quote: Hold your winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
facts.claim: Our rule for winners: sell partials into strength and trail the rising moving averages.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally.
facts.claim: Our stop moves up to breakeven once the trade is 2R to 5R ahead; we teach it at the first trim.

walkthroughs.title: Every setup carries a plan
steps: Every trade plan we teach hands you two prices: the trigger, which is the entry, and the stop.
R is your risk per share, entry to stop. A third comes off at 3R and another at 5R.
Then you trail. The stop follows the stock up, under each higher low or a rising average.

walkthroughs.title: Names and families
steps: Our catalog sorts every setup into a family. Learn the family and the name gets easier to place.
The Kicker, High Volume Edge and Gap Support are Gaps & Catalysts. Oops Reversal and Slingshot are Reversals & Reclaims.
The Launchpad sits in Bases & Breakouts. The Go Signal and the ORB are Intraday.

walkthroughs.title: A name is not an edge
steps: The textbook kicker is a down candle, then a gap up the other way.
Investopedia calls it highly reliable. Bulkowski's tests found it reversed the trend 53% of the time, almost random.
So I don't trade the name. I trade the plan: our entry, our stop, a third off at 3R and at 5R.

questions.q: In our setup plans, what is a setup's trigger?
questions.why: The setup's entry price. Each setup's plan comes with its own trigger, the entry, and its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: Trigger means entry. Every setup hands you one, plus a stop.

wrong.The setup's stop price: The stop is the other price each setup gives you. The trigger is where you get in.
wrong.The first profit target: Trims come later: a third at 3R and at 5R, sized off your entry-to-stop risk.
wrong.The news that moved it: News can be why a stock moves. The trigger is a price on the chart.

questions.q: Fill in the order our setup plans run in.
questions.why: Trim. Our plans run Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail: get in, set the stop, take some off at the targets, then trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. Every trade plan we teach runs in that order.

questions.q: In candle terms, what is a bullish kicker?
choices: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
A green candle, then a gap-down red one
One candle with a long lower wick
A small candle inside the prior range
questions.answer: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
questions.why: A red candle, then a gap-up green one. Investopedia: a bearish candle, then a bullish gap up. Bulkowski: a black candle, an upward gap, a white candle.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker: a down day, then a gap up going the other way.

wrong.A green candle, then a gap-down red one: That's the bearish kicker, the mirror image.
wrong.One candle with a long lower wick: One candle can't be a kicker. It takes two candles with a gap between them.
wrong.A small candle inside the prior range: A candle inside the day before has no gap. A kicker gaps away from the day before.

questions.q: In our setup list, what is an Oops Reversal?
choices: A gap up off a red day
A close back over a 4-day high average
A close out of a tight MA cluster
questions.why: The prior close, reclaimed intraday. The stock trades under yesterday's close, then gets back over it during the day. That reclaim is the entry, with the stop at the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Oops: it lost the prior close and took it back the same day.

wrong.A close back over a 4-day high average: That's the Slingshot's entry: the close back over the 4-day average of the highs.

questions.q: What is a Launchpad in our setup list?
choices: A close out of a tight MA cluster
A close back over a 4-day high average
A pullback that holds an old gap
A weak open that buyers turn up
questions.answer: A close out of a tight MA cluster
questions.why: A close out of a tight MA cluster. The averages bunch up, and the entry is the close that breaks out of the bunch.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad: averages squeezed together, then price closes out of the squeeze.

wrong.A close back over a 4-day high average: That's the Slingshot. Its line is a short average of the highs, not a cluster.
wrong.A pullback that holds an old gap: That's Gap Support: we buy the close as the gap holds.

questions.q: What is Gap Support in our setup list?
choices: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
Shorting a gap down off the highs
Buying the open of any gap up
Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying
questions.answer: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
questions.why: Buying a pullback that holds a gap. The stock gaps up, runs, then comes back to the gap and holds. We buy the close as it holds, with the stop at the gap top or the day's low, whichever is lower.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support: the gap holds, you buy, and the gap is your line.

wrong.Shorting a gap down off the highs: Gap Support buys. A gap down off the highs is the Bear gap lesson, and that one is measured, not traded.
wrong.Buying the open of any gap up: Gap Support waits for the gap to prove it holds. The entry is the close.
wrong.Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying: Our entry is the close while the gap still holds, not after it fills.

questions.q: In our setup list, what does HVC mean?
choices: The close of a high-volume day
The highest price of the day
A high-volume gap at the open
questions.answer: The close of a high-volume day
questions.why: The close of a high-volume day. HVC is the High Volume Edge's other name in our catalog, and that setup's entry is the high-volume close.
questions.lesson_line: HVC: where a heavy-volume day closed. That price becomes a level.

wrong.The highest price of the day: That's the high. The HVC is the close.
wrong.A high-volume gap at the open: It isn't about a gap. It's where the heavy-volume day closed.
wrong.Volume above its 50-day average: That's just above-average volume. The HVC is a price: the close of that heavy day.

questions.q: What is our Go Signal?
choices: Weak open sweeps support, then turns up
A gap up off a red day
A pullback that holds an old gap
A close out of a tight MA cluster
questions.answer: Weak open sweeps support, then turns up
questions.why: A weak open that sweeps support, then turns up. It's an intraday entry in a stock that has already shown it can move.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: a strong stock opens weak, flushes support, and buyers turn it.

wrong.A pullback that holds an old gap: That's Gap Support: we buy the close as the gap holds.

questions.q: Which of our setups enters on the close back over the 4-day average of the highs?
questions.why: Slingshot. The stock slips under that short line of the highs, then closes back over it. That close is the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot: back over the 4-day average of the highs, on the close.

wrong.Launchpad: The Launchpad closes out of a tight cluster of averages.
wrong.Oops Reversal: The Oops reclaims the prior close during the day.
wrong.Go Signal: The Go Signal buys the prior close as a weak open turns up.

questions.q: Our Oops Reversal plan puts the stop at the day's low.
questions.why: True. The entry is the prior close, reclaimed during the day, and the stop is that day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Oops: buy the reclaim, stop at the day's low.

questions.q: Fill in our line on holding winners.
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling ___ into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Partials. You sell some of the position as it runs, not all of it. The rest stays on, with the stop trailing the rising averages.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. Trail the rest.

wrong.everything: Selling it all at the first pop ends the trade. The line keeps part of it on and trails it.
wrong.half: Our first trim is a third at 3R, not half.
wrong.losers: This line is about winners: take some off into strength and trail the rest.

questions.q: Our Go Signal is an intraday entry. Its real trigger is on the 30 or 65-minute chart.
questions.why: True. The daily bar shows the footprint, but the real trigger is on the 30 or 65-minute chart.
questions.lesson_line: Spot it on the daily, time it on the 30 or 65-minute chart.

questions.q: In our trade plans, what does Trim mean?
questions.why: Taking some shares off. Our plan sells a third at 3R, another third at 5R, and keeps the last third working.
questions.lesson_line: Trim means some, not all.

wrong.Selling the whole position: That's an exit. A trim keeps part of the position on.
wrong.Cutting size before you buy: That's sizing. A trim happens after you're in and it's working.

questions.q: Our catalog sorts setups into families. Which family holds the Kicker?
questions.why: Gaps & Catalysts. It sits there with the High Volume Edge and Gap Support.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker, High Volume Edge and Gap Support all sit in Gaps & Catalysts.

wrong.Reversals & Reclaims: Fair guess, since textbooks call the kicker a reversal pattern. Our catalog files it with the gaps.
wrong.Intraday: Intraday holds the Go Signal and the ORB.

questions.q: The Oops Reversal and the Slingshot share one family in our catalog. Which?
questions.why: Reversals & Reclaims. Both take back a line the stock just lost: the prior close, or the 4-day average of the highs.
questions.lesson_line: Oops Reversal and Slingshot: both in Reversals & Reclaims.

wrong.Momentum & Trend: The Slingshot feels like momentum, but our catalog files both as reclaims.
wrong.Gaps & Catalysts: That family holds the Kicker, the High Volume Edge and Gap Support.
wrong.Intraday: The Oops happens inside one day, but it's filed as a reclaim. Intraday holds the Go Signal and the ORB.

questions.q: Our catalog files the Launchpad under Momentum & Trend.
questions.why: False. The Launchpad is in Bases & Breakouts: price closes out of a tight cluster of averages.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad: Bases & Breakouts, a close out of the averages' squeeze.

questions.q: Kicker day. The red day before it topped at $11.04. What is our entry price over that high?
questions.why: $11.05, a cent over the red day's high. That's our JBI example: 11.05 over the 11.04 high.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker entry: one cent over the red day's high.

questions.q: Finish our Gap Support stop rule.
questions.sentence: The stop is the gap top or the day's low, whichever is ___.
questions.why: Lower. Of the gap top and the day's low, the stop goes on whichever sits lower.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support stop: the lower of the gap top and the day's low.

questions.q: Which of our setups does this line belong to?
questions.sentence: In our ___ lesson, a close must stay under the gap day's high.
questions.why: Bear gap. That lesson draws one line, the gap day's high, and a close must stay under it.
questions.lesson_line: Bear gap: the line is the gap day's high.

questions.q: A stock opens under yesterday's close, then trades back above it. What's that move called?
questions.why: Red to green. Down on the day at the open, up on the day once it clears the prior close. Our Go Signal buys right there.
questions.lesson_line: Red to green: from under yesterday's close to over it, in one session.

wrong.Green to red: That's the mirror: up on the day first, then down through yesterday's close.
wrong.Bear gap: Our Bear gap is a gap down that has to stay under a line. This one came back up.

questions.q: In our trade plans, what does Trail mean?
choices: Moving the stop up behind the price
Lowering the stop for more room
questions.answer: Moving the stop up behind the price
questions.why: Moving the stop up behind the price. Ours trail under each higher low or a rising average, and a trailing stop only moves in your favor.
questions.lesson_line: Trail: the stop follows the stock up, never down.

wrong.Adding shares as it rises: That's adding to a winner, a different decision. The trail moves the stop, not the size.
wrong.Lowering the stop for more room: That's widening the stop. A trail only ever tightens.

questions.q: Our Kicker has two entries. Besides the break over the red day's high, what is the other?
choices: A break of day one's 30-minute range
A close over the 4-day average of highs
A pullback that holds the gap
questions.answer: A break of day one's 30-minute range
questions.why: A break of day one's 30-minute range. That's the Kicker ORB, the opening-range break on the 30-minute chart. Day traders often use the first half hour's range the same way.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker entries: over the red day's high, or the day-one 30-minute range break.

wrong.A pullback that holds the gap: That's Gap Support, weeks after a gap. The Kicker is the gap day itself.

questions.q: On a Slingshot, our entry is the first intraday touch of the 4-day average of the highs.
questions.why: False. The entry is the close back over the 4-day average of the highs. A touch during the day isn't the signal.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot waits for the close over the line, not a touch.

questions.q: When a High Volume Edge bar closes down, our stop is still the bar's low.
questions.why: False. Our plan uses the edge bar's low, or its high when the bar closed down. A stop above the price is a buy stop, the kind that guards a short.
questions.lesson_line: Up close: stop at the bar's low. Down close: stop at its high, the short side's stop.

questions.q: Our app defines a full short trade for the Bear gap: entry, stop and targets.
questions.why: False. No trade is defined for it, and none is invented. The lesson measures the fall and the line a close must stay under.
questions.lesson_line: No plan in the app, no plan invented. The Bear gap is studied, not traded.

questions.q: Our plan names the size of the first trim, not just the level: a third at 3R.
questions.why: True. The hard rule is a third at 3R. Another third goes at 5R, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R. The plan names the size, not just the level.

questions.q: Which pair of our setups both sit in the Intraday family?
questions.why: Go Signal and ORB. Both are timed inside the day: the Go Signal on the 30 or 65-minute chart, the ORB off the opening range.
questions.lesson_line: The Go Signal and the ORB are both Intraday setups.

wrong.Launchpad and High Volume Edge: The Launchpad is Bases & Breakouts. The High Volume Edge is Gaps & Catalysts.

questions.story: Yesterday a stock opened at $20.50 and closed red at $20.00, near its low. Its high was $20.60. Today it opens at $20.55 and trades up through $20.60.
questions.q: Which setup of ours is this?
questions.why: Kicker. A red day, then a gap up over its close and a push through its high. Our entry is over that high, at market as it trades through.
questions.lesson_line: Red day, gap up, through its high: that's a Kicker.

wrong.Oops Reversal: The Oops trades under the prior close and reclaims it. This one opened above it.
wrong.Gap Support: Gap Support is a later pullback that holds an old gap. This is the gap day itself.
wrong.Slingshot: The Slingshot closes back over the 4-day average of the highs. This is a gap up off a red day.

questions.story: A stock closed at $30.00 yesterday, with a low of $29.20. Today it opens at $29.60 and trades down to $29.00. By midday it's back at $30.05.
questions.q: Which setup of ours fits?
questions.why: Oops Reversal. It lost yesterday's close, even undercut yesterday's low, then took the close back during the day. That reclaim of $30.00 is the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Under the prior close, back over it the same day: Oops.

wrong.Kicker: A Kicker gaps up off a red day. This one opened weak.
wrong.Bear gap: A Bear gap is a gap down that stays under its line. This one came all the way back.
wrong.Launchpad: Nothing here is about a cluster of averages.

questions.q: Oops Reversal: you buy the reclaim of yesterday's $30.00 close. The day's low is $29.00. Where is our first trim, 3R?
questions.why: $33.00. Entry minus stop is a dollar a share. Three of those on top of $30.00 is 3R, where a third comes off.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is three times your entry-to-stop risk, added to the entry.

questions.story: A stock's short-term, 21-day and 50-day averages have bunched tightly together. Price has sat just on top of the bunch for days. Today it closes higher, out of the cluster.
questions.q: What is our name for this setup?
questions.why: Launchpad. The averages are bunched tight, and today's close breaks out of the cluster. That close is the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Tight cluster of averages, then a close out of it: Launchpad.

wrong.Slingshot: The Slingshot's line is the 4-day average of the highs, not a squeeze of longer averages.
wrong.Gap Support: There's no gap in this story.
wrong.High Volume Edge: Nothing says the volume was heavy. The cluster of averages is the tell.

questions.story: You're long a Kicker. It pulled back to $31 and rallied. Now it has pulled back again, held $33, and turned up.
questions.q: Trailing under each higher low, where does the stop go now?
questions.why: Just under $33. That's the new, higher low, so the stop moves up under it. A break of it would end the run of higher lows.
questions.lesson_line: Each new higher low pulls the stop up behind it.

wrong.Just under $31: That was the last higher low. $33 has replaced it.
wrong.Back under the Kicker's low: That's where the stop started. Trailing means it has moved up since.
wrong.At today's close: The plan trails under the low, not at the close.

questions.q: On the daily bar, what shows buyers stepped in on a Go Signal?
choices: A lower wick of 40% of the range
An upper wick of 40% of the range
A gap up over the prior high
questions.answer: A lower wick of 40% of the range
questions.why: A lower wick of 40% of the range, or the low under the open with the close in the upper half. Sellers pushed it down and buyers took it back.
questions.lesson_line: Long lower wick, strong close: buyers showed up after the flush.

wrong.An upper wick of 40% of the range: An upper wick means it was pushed down from the high. That's the opposite.
wrong.A gap up over the prior high: A Go Signal opens weak, under the prior close. No gap up.
wrong.Volume at twice its average: Twice-average volume belongs to the recent-move check, the 4% gap. It isn't the buyers check.

questions.q: Our Launchpad plan trails the stop under the 4-day average of the highs.
questions.why: False. The Launchpad trails under the rising 21-day average, or under each higher low. The 4-day average of the highs is the Slingshot's entry line.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad trail: the rising 21-day average, or each higher low.

questions.story: The gap top is $50.00. Today the stock dipped to $49.60, then closed at $52.00. You buy that close as Gap Support.
questions.q: Where does our stop go?
questions.why: $49.60, today's low. Our stop is the gap top or the day's low, whichever is lower, and today's low sits under the gap top.
questions.lesson_line: Two candidates, take the lower one. That's the Gap Support stop.

wrong.$50.00, the gap top: That's the higher of the two here. Our rule takes the lower.
wrong.3.5% under your entry: That's part of the Kicker's stop rule, not Gap Support's.

questions.story: You buy our Kicker at $40.00. The Kicker candle's low is $39.20.
questions.q: Where does our stop go?
questions.why: Under the Kicker low. It's only 2% under your $40.00 entry, closer than 3.5%. Our rule takes whichever is closer.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker stop: the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under entry, whichever is closer.

wrong.3.5% under your entry: That's the other half of the rule. Here the Kicker's low is closer, so it wins.
wrong.Under the red day's low: The red day came before the Kicker. Our stop hangs off the Kicker candle itself.

questions.story: You buy a Slingshot on the close. The trigger day's low is $52.10. The day before, the low was $51.40.
questions.q: You want more room than our standard stop. Which stop does the plan allow?
choices: Under the 4-day average of the highs
questions.why: $51.40, the day before's low. Our standard stop is the trigger day's low, and the day before's low is the wider choice.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot stop: the trigger day's low, or the day before's low for more room.

wrong.$52.10, the trigger day's low: That's the standard stop, the tighter one.
wrong.Under the 4-day average of the highs: That line is the entry, not the stop.
wrong.Under the 50-day average: Not in the Slingshot plan. Its stops are the two daily lows.

questions.story: Weeks ago a stock closed at $64 on its heaviest volume in a year. It ran to $75. Now, for the first time, it's back at $64.20.
questions.q: In our High Volume Edge plan, what is this spot?
questions.why: The cleanest decision point. The first return to the high-volume close is where our plan says to decide.
questions.lesson_line: First return to the high-volume close: the cleanest place to decide.

wrong.A failed setup: sell now: Nothing has failed yet. It's back at the level, and that's where you decide.
wrong.The 3R target: Targets are measured up from the entry. This is a pullback to the entry level.
wrong.A new Kicker: A Kicker needs a red day and a gap up. This is a return to an old close.

questions.story: You bought Gap Support at $82 as the gap held. Since the gap, the stock's best price was $90. It's heading back up there now.
questions.q: What does our plan say about $90?
choices: Where we first take some off
Where to move the stop up
Where to add a few more shares
questions.answer: Where we first take some off
questions.why: The first place to take some off. In our Gap Support plan, the post-gap high is the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support: trim first at the post-gap high.

wrong.Where to move the stop up: The stop stays down at the gap. The post-gap high is a trim spot.
wrong.Where to add a few more shares: Adding there isn't in the plan. It's where we take some off.
wrong.Sell the whole position there: Trim means some, not all. Keep the rest working.

questions.q: Once you trail a stop up, you move it back down if the stock dips.
questions.why: False. A trailing stop only moves in your favor. When price moves against you, the stop stays where it is.
questions.lesson_line: A trail tightens. It never widens.

questions.story: A strong stock closed at $40.00 yesterday. Today it opens at $39.10, dips under yesterday's low, then climbs. By 11 a.m. it trades $40.00.
questions.q: Where is our Go Signal entry?
questions.why: $40.00, the prior close. It traded there this session, red to green, so that's the entry. The stop is the session's low.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal entry: the prior close, the moment it goes red to green.

wrong.$39.10, today's open: Buying the weak open is guessing. We wait for the turn back to the prior close.
wrong.Today's close, wherever it ends: That's the fallback, only when it never trades back to the prior close.

questions.q: Launchpad. The 21-day average is $48.00, the 50-day is $47.50, and the ATR is $2.00. Where does our stop go?
questions.why: $47.00. The lower average is the 50-day at $47.50. A quarter of the $2.00 ATR below it is $47.00.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad stop: a quarter of an ATR under the lower of the 21-day and 50-day.

questions.story: You buy a setup at $60 with its stop at $57. It reaches $69 and keeps going.
questions.q: Counting in R, where is it on our plan?
questions.why: At 3R. The risk was $3 a share, $60 down to $57. It's up $9, three times that risk. That's the first trim: a third off, stop to breakeven.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R: the gain divided by your entry-to-stop risk.

wrong.At 5R: the second trim: 5R needs five times the risk. This is three.
wrong.At 9R: nine dollars up: That's dollars, not R. Divide the $9 gain by the $3 risk.

questions.q: Why does a huge-volume day's close become a level worth watching?
choices: Heavy volume usually marks a top
Volume shows the next day's direction
questions.why: Big volume usually means institutions. IBD says large volume jumps are usually institutions buying or selling, and Investopedia says big traders create big volume. Our High Volume Edge buys that day's close, the HVC.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume leaves a footprint. The close of that day is a level.

wrong.Heavy volume usually marks a top: Not usually. Investopedia says breakouts on high volume are more likely to keep going.
wrong.Volume shows the next day's direction: Volume shows who was active, not what tomorrow does.

questions.q: Our trims sit at 3R and 5R. What is 1R?
choices: Your risk per share, entry to stop
questions.answer: Your risk per share, entry to stop
questions.why: Your risk per share, entry to stop. Tharp's example: buy at $50 with the exit at $40, and 1R is $10. Our 3R and 5R trims count in those units.
questions.lesson_line: 1R is your risk per share. The targets count up in those units.

wrong.1% of your account: That's an account-risk number. R is per share: the gap from your entry to your stop.
wrong.The first profit target: That's 3R in our plan, the first trim. 1R is the unit the trims are measured in.
wrong.A 1% move in the stock: R isn't a percent move. It's the dollars per share between entry and stop.

questions.q: A setup fires with its trigger at $45.00 and its stop at $43.50. Where is our 3R target?
questions.why: $49.50. Three times the trigger-to-stop risk, added to the $45.00 trigger.
questions.lesson_line: 3R: three times your risk per share, on top of the entry.

questions.story: A strong stock with a rising 20-day opens under yesterday's close and sweeps yesterday's low. The day's range is $48.00 to $50.00. It closes at $48.60.
questions.q: Is this a Go Signal day?
choices: No: it closed 30% up its range
Yes: weak open, then a sweep
questions.answer: No: it closed 30% up its range
questions.why: No. A Go Signal day closes in the upper 40% of its range. $48.60 is only 30% of the way up from $48.00 to $50.00.
questions.lesson_line: No strong close, no Go Signal. The close has to land in the top 40% of the range.

wrong.Yes: weak open, then a sweep: Those are two of the checks. The close must also sit in the top 40% of the range, and 30% doesn't.
wrong.Yes: the 20-day is rising: That's the first check, not the last. A close 30% up the range fails the strong-close check.

questions.story: Three stocks open under yesterday's close, sweep yesterday's low, and close near their highs. A: 20-day average falling. B: up 15% in five sessions two weeks ago, 20-day rising. C: flat for months, 20-day flat.
questions.q: Which one fits our Go Signal?
questions.why: Stock B. Our Go Signal needs a rising 20-day average and a notable recent move, like a 13% gain over 5 sessions within the last 20. Only B has both.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: strength first, then the weak open and the turn.

wrong.Stock A: A falling 20-day fails the first check. A turn inside a downtrend isn't a Go Signal.
wrong.Stock C: A flat 20-day fails the rising-average check.

questions.story: A Go Signal day. The stock opens under yesterday's $25.00 close, sweeps support, and buyers turn it. It closes strong at $24.90, never trading $25.00.
questions.q: Where is our entry?
choices: Skip it: no red to green
questions.why: The close, $24.90. Our entry is the prior close when it trades that session. When it never gets there, the entry is the close.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: the prior close if it trades, otherwise the close.

wrong.Yesterday's close, $25.00: It never traded there today, so there's no fill at $25.00.
wrong.Today's weak open: The weak open comes before the turn. We don't buy the weakness.
wrong.Skip it: no red to green: Red to green is the first entry, not a must. The plan falls back to the close.

questions.story: VRNS opened 37% down on a gap and closed at the low. A short's obvious stop, the gap day's high, sat 25% over the close.
questions.q: Why does our lesson study this fall instead of shorting it?
choices: The honest stop is far too wide
Gap downs fill, so it will bounce
It closed at the low, so it's done
questions.answer: The honest stop is far too wide
questions.why: The honest stop is far too wide. It sat 25% over the close, so no trade was invented. The lesson measures the fall and the line a close must stay under.
questions.lesson_line: If the honest stop is 25% away, there's no trade. Study it instead.

wrong.Gap downs fill, so it will bounce: Whether the gap fills isn't the reason. The lesson skips the trade because the stop is 25% away.
wrong.It closed at the low, so it's done: That isn't the reason. The lesson still measures the fall. The problem is the 25% stop.

questions.q: In Bulkowski's tests, how often did the bullish kicking candle reverse the trend?
questions.why: Close to a coin flip. Bulkowski found it reversed the trend 53% of the time, which he calls almost random. Investopedia calls kickers highly reliable; his numbers say otherwise.
questions.lesson_line: A candle's name isn't an edge. The plan around it is.

wrong.A reversal almost every time: That's the kicker's reputation, and Investopedia calls it highly reliable. Bulkowski's tests found 53%.
wrong.It almost never reverses: Not that either. 53% is about even.

questions.story: Your Gap Support trade hasn't gone anywhere. For a week the stock drifts sideways right at the gap.
questions.q: What does our plan do with the stop?
choices: Tighten it to just under the gap top
Widen it to give the trade room
questions.answer: Tighten it to just under the gap top
questions.why: Tighten it to just under the gap top. When it drifts sideways at the gap, our plan tightens the stop there.
questions.lesson_line: A trade going nowhere at the gap gets a tighter stop, not more room.

wrong.Widen it to give the trade room: Widening adds risk to a trade that isn't working.
wrong.Leave it and wait for 3R: The plan says to tighten when it drifts at the gap. Waiting with the wide stop keeps more risk on.

questions.story: Six weeks ago a stock gapped up on big volume and never filled the gap. Now it has pulled back to the top of the gap and is holding.
questions.q: Which of our setups is this?
questions.why: Gap Support. The gap is still open and the pullback is holding it. We buy the close as it holds, with the stop at the gap top or the day's low, whichever is lower.
questions.lesson_line: An old gap that holds on the pullback: Gap Support.

wrong.Kicker: A Kicker is the gap day itself, off a red day. This is weeks later.
wrong.Oops Reversal: The Oops reclaims the prior close inside one day. This is about an old gap.
wrong.Bear gap: A Bear gap is a gap down. This one gapped up.

questions.story: A stock closes up at $72 on its heaviest volume in a year. That day's low was $68.
questions.q: Where are our High Volume Edge entry and stop?
choices: Entry over the day's high, stop $68
questions.why: Entry $72, stop $68. We buy the high-volume close and put the stop at the edge bar's low, since it closed up.
questions.lesson_line: High Volume Edge: buy the high-volume close, stop at the edge bar's low.

wrong.Entry next day's open, stop $68: The entry is the high-volume close itself, not the next open.
wrong.Entry over the day's high, stop $68: That's breakout-style buying. Our entry is the close.
wrong.Entry $72, stop 3.5% under: The 3.5% stop is part of the Kicker's rule. Here the stop is the edge bar's low.

questions.q: Investopedia's opening range is the first 15 minutes. Our Kicker ORB uses that same window.
questions.why: False. Ours is the 30-minute opening range on day one. Investopedia notes many day traders use the first half hour too.
questions.lesson_line: Our Kicker ORB: the first 30 minutes, on day one.

questions.q: On our plan, a setup that reaches 3R is done: you sell it all there.
questions.why: False. 3R is the first trim: a third comes off and the stop moves to breakeven. Another third goes at 5R, and the last third trails.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is a trim, not the finish line.

questions.q: On a Go Signal day, the low sweeps support. Which of these levels counts?
questions.why: The 5-bar low. Our list: the prior low, the 5-bar low, or a 9, 20 or 50-day average the prior close was above.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal sweeps: the prior low, the 5-bar low, or the 9, 20 or 50-day average.

wrong.The 200-day average: Our list stops at the 9, 20 and 50-day averages. The 200-day isn't on it.
wrong.Yesterday's close: That's the line it reclaims for the entry, red to green. The sweep happens lower.

questions.story: Your note reads: 'Slingshot. Entry on the close back over the 4-day average of the highs. Stop under the trigger day's low. Trail under the 4-day line.'
questions.q: One line in the note doesn't match our plan. Which?
choices: Entry on the close back over it
Stop under the trigger day's low
questions.why: Trail under the 4-day line. Our Slingshot trails under the 10-day average or each higher low. The 4-day average of the highs is the entry line.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot: enter over the 4-day highs line, trail the 10-day or the higher lows.

wrong.Entry on the close back over it: That's our entry, word for word.
wrong.Stop under the trigger day's low: That's our stop. The day before's low is the wider choice.

questions.story: A stock gaps down hard off its highs. Eight days later it closes above the gap day's high.
questions.q: In our Bear gap lesson, what does that close mean?
choices: It broke the gap day's high
The Bear gap is still on track
It's a fresh Bear gap setup
questions.answer: It broke the gap day's high
questions.why: It broke the line. Our lesson's line is the gap day's high, and a close must stay under it.
questions.lesson_line: Bear gap: a close over the gap day's high breaks it.

wrong.The Bear gap is still on track: Not after a close over the gap day's high. That's the one line it had to stay under.
wrong.It's a fresh Bear gap setup: A Bear gap is a gap down. This is a close back up through the line.

questions.story: A stock closed at $50.00 yesterday. Today it opens at $49.20, dips to $48.80, and closes at $49.60. It never trades back to $50.00.
questions.q: Did our Oops Reversal trigger?
choices: Yes: it bounced off the low
Yes: it closed in the upper half
questions.why: No. Our Oops entry is the prior close, reclaimed during the day. It bounced, but it never got back to $50.00.
questions.lesson_line: A bounce isn't a reclaim. No prior close, no Oops.

wrong.Yes: it bounced off the low: A bounce off the low isn't the trigger. The reclaim of the prior close is.
wrong.Yes: it closed in the upper half: A strong close is one of the Go Signal's checks. The Oops needs the prior close back.

questions.q: On a Slingshot, our stop is the trigger day's low.
questions.why: True. The stop is the trigger day's low. The day before's low is the wider choice.
questions.lesson_line: Slingshot stop: the trigger day's low.

conflicts: Older wording elsewhere in the repo defines two of these setups differently: the vocab.method glossary bank (recall.glossary.json) and the skill_map lesson_key slugs call the Go Signal 'a catalyst gap digests into the 9 EMA, then engulfs' and the Launchpad 'a tight base on top of stacked moving averages'. TRADE_PLANS.md (2026-11-08, read from the detectors and the owner's rulings) defines the Go Signal as a weak open that sweeps support and turns, and the Launchpad entry as the close out of the tight cluster of averages. docs/study/research/definitions.json also defines the Go Signal differently, as an intraday confirmation that a planned entry is live. This unit follows TRADE_PLANS.md only and never uses lesson_key slugs or the older glossary as a source. The owner may want the old glossary items retired.

Kicker: the textbook shape is narrower than our detector. Investopedia's bullish kicker opens at or beyond the first candle's open; Bulkowski's bullish kicking is two marubozu candles with an upward gap. Our uct_kicker detector fires on a weak prior close, an open above the prior close and a trade through the prior high. The unit teaches the shape 'in candle terms' (q03, from two Tier 2 publishers) and our plan from TRADE_PLANS.md; it never says our Kicker needs marubozu candles. q28's story fits both (it opens above the red day's open and trades through its high).

Kicker reliability: Investopedia calls kickers 'rare but highly reliable'; Bulkowski measured the bullish kicking at 53% ('almost random'). Asked only as what each source says (q51, w3), never as a prediction.

Opening range window: Investopedia defines the opening range on the first 15 minutes and notes day traders often use the first half hour. Our Kicker ORB is the 30-minute range (the owner's ruling). q55 asks it as ours.

Gap definition: Investopedia (breakaway gap page) measures a gap from the prior close to the open; Bulkowski requires today's low above yesterday's high. No question here quizzes a general gap definition; Gap Support's 'gap top' and the Bear gap line are taken from TRADE_PLANS.md.

Oops Reversal: Larry Williams's classic Oops (open below the prior day's low, then a buy back at that low) differs from ours (the prior close, reclaimed during the day; the detector also wants an undercut of the prior low). No reliable page for Williams's version could be read (definitions.json records a 403 on the magazine article; this session's web search budget ran out), so only our version is taught.

High Volume Edge on a down close: TRADE_PLANS.md gives the stop as 'its high on a down close' (the detector reads a down-close edge bar as bearish). q24 asks only what the stop is, not how to trade the short side.

The Oops Reversal and the Go Signal share the same entry mechanic (the prior close, reclaimed in the session). TRADE_PLANS.md lists the Go Signal's checks but not the Oops's, so no question says what one needs that the other does not, and no question offers both as choices where both would fit.

HVC: skill_map.json lists HVC only as an alias of the High Volume Edge. q07 reads it as the high-volume close from TRADE_PLANS.md's entry wording; the detector's docstring (uct_hve.py, not a citable source) says the same: 'the high-volume close (HVC)'.

Gap top: TRADE_PLANS.md uses 'the gap top' without defining it (uct_gap_support.py takes it as the prior day's high, the top of the range before the gap). No question asks what the gap top is; questions give it as a price.

R and the trims: until 2026-11-09 TRADE_PLANS.md put the detectors' targets 'at 2R and 3R from that stop' and named no fraction; the owner's account rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9, B19, E51) replaces it with a third at 3R (stop to breakeven), a third at 5R, the last third trailed, and TRADE_PLANS.md was rewritten to match. R is still taken from the Van Tharp Institute (initial risk per share, entry to stop); every trim calc here is entry + 3 x (entry - stop).

Checker, 2026-11-09: q24 now names the down-close stop as a short's stop. TRADE_PLANS.md puts the stop at the edge bar's high on a down close with the entry at the close, which only works as a short; Investor.gov (t22, t23) says a buy stop sits above the price and guards a short. Without that line a member could read it as a stop above a long entry.

Gap, two senses (track audit 2026-11-09): V.02 q50 defines a chart gap as no overlap between two days' ranges (ChartSchool, Bulkowski). Our Kicker detector (uct_kicker.py, rule K2) calls an open over the prior close a gap up, even inside the prior range, and q28's open ($20.55) sits over the $20.00 close but under the $20.60 high. q28's why now says 'a gap up over its close' so the sense is named; V.02 q50's wrong note now says 'On a chart'.
